catalog_locator: Hyman 1981: abstract p.169; sec. 2 'An Accentual Approach' p.177; sec. 3 'Accent Assignment' p.178; sec. 6 p.198
catalog_quote: In this paper it is demonstrated that Somali is a tonal accent language, i.e. a language which (a) assigns accents to vowels (rather than syllables), and (b) realizes these accents as an invariant H tone. The language also allows, under specifiable conditions, words totally lacking an accent, another common characteristic of tonal accent languages. The model developed in this study includes rules of accent placement (on either the final or penultimate vowel of a word), accent modification (shifts, reductions), and tone and pitch assignment. ... The above discussion indicates that although Somali has H and L tone (with a mid level being predictable from the surrounding context), the distribution of one of these tones, the H tone, is extremely limited: a word can have only one H tone, and this H tone can occur only on a penultimate or final vowel. ... the occurrence and location of accent…
sweep_summary: Somali (soma1255) is coded 'tonal' from Hyman 1981 (held, re-read, verbatim). The 13 title hits reduce to 10 distinct works (Orwin 1996 appears three times, Andrzejewski 1956 twice). Newly downloaded and read: Downing & Nilsson 2019 (Language Science Press, open) - confirms: one culminative H per minimal PWord on the penult or final mora, Somali 'a tonal language, not an (underlyingly) accentual one'; Biber 1982 (SAL 13(1), open) - primary data on Central Somali (= Maay, maay1238: tonal accent shifted one mora rightward) and a restatement of Hyman for Northern Somali - confirms, and is a second source for the maay1238 reclassify flagged in our check; bonus Green 2022 (Afrika und Uebersee, CC BY) - confirms (H on penultimate mora in masculine stems, final mora in feminine stems). Abstract/extract only: Andrzejewski 1956 BSOAS (paywalled; p.103 extract on tone-gender correlation in the Isaaq dialect). Not obtainable: Orwin 1996 moraic model (Routledge DOI paywalled, archive.org lending copy restricted; medium priority), Green & Morrison 2016 (Springer closed; medium), Andrzejewski 1984 (Benjamins; low), Orwin 2001 on metrics (verse prosody; low), Johnson 1979 Horn of Africa (print only, content unverified; low), Hyman 1981 Italian version (print only, duplicate of the English text we hold; none). Nothing read contradicts the classification; best new statement is Downing & Nilsson 2019 p.125, which does not supersede Hyman 1981 but is the best modern open co-citation.archive.

new_statements.quote: It is uncontroversial that the Somali tonal system has canonical stress-like properties, as defined in Downing (2010) and Hyman (2006; 2011; 2012; 2014). Work by Hyman (1981; 2006; 2012); Le Gac (2003); Green & Morrison (2016), and Saeed (2004) agrees that High tone is culminative: no more than one High tone can occur per (minimal Phonological) Word (PWord). The position of High tones is, roughly, demarcative: they occur on either the penult or final mora of a PWord. Only some proper names have a High tone in another position (Saeed 1999: 22). [...] However, we do assume that Somali is a tonal language, not an (underlyingly) accentual one.

new_statements.reading: A 2019 peer-reviewed, open-access, elicitation-based study by two Somali prosody specialists states the consensus of the whole later literature: Somali word prosody is a culminative High tone (at most one per minimal Phonological Word) restricted to the penult or final mora, positioned by morphology; the language is tonal, not stress-accented. This matches the catalog's 'tonal' coding and its domain note exactly.

sources.note: Re-read in the OA text we hold: Somali has no stress; a single H-tone accent per word on the final or penultimate vowel (mora), placement governed by morphology (gender, number, verb class); some words accentless. This is the catalog's deciding source and its quotation is verbatim.

sources.quote: Abstract: 'argues that there is no one High tone per word rule in Somali ... the one High tone per word rule does not extend to loanwords and therefore is not productive.' Treats Somali prosody as H tone (tonal), challenging only the synchronic status of word-level culminativity — touches our domain_quote ('a word can have only one H tone') but not the TONAL-OR-PITCH-ACCENT class.
sources.note: Directly disputes the 'one H per word' culminativity statement that our domain=word coding quotes (loanword evidence); needed to decide whether the domain note should carry a caveat. Does not affect the tonal classification.

sources.quote: As has been long established in seminal works on Somali phonology like Hyman (1981) and Banti (1988a), the examples in (1) show that lexical stems exhibit a single high (H) tone on either their penultimate or final vocalic mora. [...] Words like those in (1) illustrate long-noted correlations between H tone location and grammatical gender in noun stems, with H being associated with the penultimate vocalic mora in masculine or 'k-series' grammatical gender stems and instead with the final vocalic mora in feminine or 't-series' gender stems.
sources.note: By the author of the 2021 De Gruyter Somali Grammar: one H tone per lexical stem on the penultimate (masculine/k-series) or final (feminine/t-series) vocalic mora; toneless vowels realised low; footnote 4 surveys competing analyses (Hyman 1981 declension class; Nilsson 2018 stem shape; Godon 1998, Lampitelli 2011/2013, Le Gac 1997 catalectic slot with H always on the penultimate mora). No stress mentioned for Somali. Coda consonants do not count as tone-bearing moras.

sources.note: Word prosody = one culminative High tone per minimal Phonological Word on the penult or final mora, position set by morphology (declension class, gender, number), not phonology; authors treat Somali as tonal, not underlyingly accentual; the paper's contribution is that determiners/modifiers variably lose their expected H through prosodic restructuring (PWord adjunction), paralleling Swedish. Elicitation-based corpus (997 N+determiner, 599 N+modifier tokens).
